prompt:
You are the single most hostile representative of a U.S. federal statistical agency
in the room at a working group. Someone has built a "readiness diagnostic" that rates your
agency's public website on whether machines can reach, read and use the data you publish, and is
about to show the room the item below. Read it as that hostile representative — skeptical,
protective of your agency, alert to being made to look bad — and answer three questions bluntly
and specifically, quoting the item's words where you can:

1. What in this item would you OBJECT to: a claim you find unfair or wrong, or that makes your
   agency look bad for something you would say is not your fault or not your doing?
2. What WORD or phrase here would you, or a non-technical colleague, not understand?
3. What would you say we are SECRETLY DOING: what hidden agenda, trap, or gotcha would you
   suspect behind this item?

Answer only from the item. For each question, "raised" is "yes" if you have a real objection /
an unclear word / a suspicion, and "no" if you genuinely have none. Return ONLY a JSON object,
no prose before or after and no code fence:
{"object_to": {"raised": "yes" or "no", "text": "..."}, "word_not_understood": {"raised": "yes" or "no", "text": "..."}, "secretly_doing": {"raised": "yes" or "no", "text": "..."}}

ITEM (check Page links a methodology readable as text)
CHECK: Page links a methodology readable as text

How this check counts: Shown for transparency, not scored as a finding about the agency: at least one part of this check rests on a rule this project chose, not a published standard.
The question: Can a machine reach the methodology behind the data and read it as plain text, without having to run scripts?
Where we look: The data product page itself, and any link on it whose web address or wording contains the word "methodology" (up to twenty-five such links).
What the client does: The public client opens the data page and then opens each of those methodology links to read what the document actually sends.
What passing looks like: Every data page that was looked at links to a methodology document served as a web page or plain text, readable before any script runs, with enough text and not mostly links.
What partial, fail and not measured look like: Partial — Some of the agency's data pages that were looked at met this and some did not. Fail — For every data page looked at, no methodology link (up to twenty-five followed) led to a document meeting the project's text measures: at least two thousand visible characters before any script runs and no more than a quarter of the text sitting in links. A short but readable page, or a chapter hub, can fall short of those measures. It is not a claim that the methodology needs scripts or cannot be read, nor that the agency publishes no methodology: one linked under another name, such as "technical documentation" or "about the data", is simply not found. Not measured — The public client could not finish looking at one or more pages, for one of three reasons: the host turned the identified client away; the client's own honoring of the site's robots.txt stopped it reading the page; or a server or network error, or methodology links it could not follow, left the result unconfirmed.
Why it matters: A published guide on readable data documentation asks that text documentation, methodology included, be reachable by people and by web crawlers, and an OMB memo asks agencies to default web content to a plain web page rather than another format. The added rule that the text be readable before any script runs is the project's own reading of "reachable by crawlers", since many crawlers do not run scripts.
Who else runs this check: No public tool runs this exact check.
What rung two changes: Nothing: this check needs no key.
